headlines.article_text: Meta (META) Q3 2026 earnings report: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 4:22 04:22 Meta's AI bet faces Wall Street Closing Bell Meta is slated to report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, and investors will be looking for signs that the company's latest artificial intelligence efforts will bolster future sales. Here's what analysts polled by LSEG are expecting: Earnings per share : $5.75 Revenue : $63.2 billion It's been a big quarter for Mark Zuckerberg's company due to the initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September and shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022. Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday. Wall Street will likely be monitoring for whether Meta plans to increase its data center-related capital expenditures, or capex, to further develop the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models. The company revealed in July during its second-quarter earnings that it narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to come in between $130 billion and $145 billion, representing a $5 billion increase to the low end of its prior range. All that spending resulted in Meta's free cash flow in the period shrinking to $784 million from $8.55 billion in the same quarter a year earlier. Analysts expect Meta's capex to swell to $196.3 billion in 2027, according to FactSet. Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, is expected to come in at 3.65 billion, according to StreetAccount, almost flat from the prior quarter. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta is offering $20 and $100 monthly subscription plans for Muse AI agent power users. Right now, Muse is free to use but requires a subscription to run it with Meta's latest model — Muse Wonder . The company is also charging developers $50 or $200 a month to access its most powerful Muse Wonder Full AI model via the Muse coding agent that debuted in early August. Meta's nascent subscription efforts represent opportunities for the company to expand beyond online advertising , which is still its core money maker. Investors have been concerned about the Facebook parent's hefty AI investments relative to rivals like Alphabet and Amazon that have cloud computing businesses . While AI-specific monetization efforts offer hope of diversification, they remains a longer-term play. Last week, Meta teamed up with longtime rival Apple to make Meta's new open-weight AI model work with the iPhone maker's high-end Mac computers. Unlike Meta's proprietary AI models, coders can download the weights of Muse Spark Open for free . Meta is betting that developers who try Muse Spark Open may eventually want to pay to access the company's more powerful proprietary AI systems. "These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said in an interview with CNBC. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage." — Jonathan Vanian 5 Min Ago Meta Reality Labs expected to continue bleeding money Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive officer of Meta Platforms Inc., left, and Andrew Bosworth, chief technology officer and head of Reality Labs, wear Meta Ray-Ban Display AI glasses during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Meta's Reality Labs division, which is tasked with developing virtual reality headsets and AI-powered wearable devices, is expected to post a loss of $4.54 billion while generating $513 million in sales for the third quarter, according to StreetAccount. In July when Meta reported second-quarter earnings , the company revealed that the Reality Labs unit lost $4.62 billion while bringing in $431 million during the period. With the VR market struggling to catch on with consumers , Zuckerberg has since shifted Reality Labs resources to center on more on AI-driven hardware products like the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses the company creates with eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica . Still, Zuckerberg hasn't completely abandoned VR and its sibling technology augmented reality. The CEO revealed in September during the company's annual Connect conference for developers the Meta VR Glasses , which will cost $1,299 then they are released in the spring of 2027. "We have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion, high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time," Zuckerberg said at the time. — Jonathan Vanian 9 Min Ago Meta still depends heavily on online advertising Wall Street may be pleased that Meta's AI strategy involves subscription pushes and potential new revenue opportunities , but it will take a while before those efforts pay off. Until then, the company's massive online advertising business continues to be its financial anchor. Meta is expected to report third-quarter advertising revenue of $61.87 billion. The social media giant said in July that it posted $59.36 billion in second-quarter ad sales. — Jonathan Vanian 1 Hour Ago Cambridge Analytica still haunts Zuckerberg The Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago continues to haunt Zuckerberg and his social media empire. New Mexico district court judge Francis Mathew imposed a $25 billion penalty on Meta today over a state data privacy case that derived from 2018 privacy revelations. The fine, revealed in a court filing, came after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse determined that the company formally known as Facebook should be held liable for misleading New Mexico residents about its data handling practices and methods to prevent harmful information from spreading on its family of apps. Although New Mexico was awarded $219.5 billion, based on the social media company committing over 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, the judge reduced that figure to $25 billion. "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations, judge Mathew wrote in the filing, regarding the company's then pledge to examine the "data misuse." — Jonathan Vanian 2 Hours Ago What analyst expect with Meta's Muse and AI agents Muse signage during a preview event ahead of Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. headlines.article_text: GM aims to shorten vehicle development time with AI, software push Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. In this article GM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:20 04:20 Highlights from GM Forward 2026 Power Lunch NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses. He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad. "There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise." Next-generation vehicles GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles – regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them. "We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them." AI development GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed. "This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release. General Motors CEO Mary Barra (left), Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and President Mark Reuss at the company's GM Forward event in downtown Manhattan on Oct. 21, 2026. Michael Wayland | CNBC GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development. The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype. Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028. Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar. "In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools." In-vehicle AI The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers. GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand. The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models. GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle. The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system. headlines.summary: Rick Rieder, BlackRock's CIO of global fixed income, lays out his expectations for the fourth quarter and where he sees the best opportunities.
headlines.article_text: Rick Rieder sees historic opportunity in investment-grade bonds Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points BlackRock's Rick Rieder is bullish on this area of the credit market for the first time in a "long time." The CIO of global fixed income lays out his fourth-quarter fixed-income outlook in an exclusive interview. In this article BLK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026. Aaron Clamage | CNBC Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance." While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit. iShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to date Best opportunities include hyperscalers Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised. "Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield." Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be." The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out. Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026 Fed watch Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool . The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said. "They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure." Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks ahead Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026. "The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said. Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on." In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said. headlines.title: Almadex Expands Claim Block at New Hope, Provides Exploration Update
headlines.summary: VANCOUVER, British Columbia, Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Almadex Minerals Ltd. headlines.article_text: Meta ordered to pay $25B in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal in New Mexico. The penalty comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.
